questions.prompt: Why does a saturated MOSFET's drain current keep rising slightly with \(V_{DS}\)?
options: The pinch-off point moves toward the source, so the effective channel gets shorter
questions.explanation: The drain depletion region widens, \(L_{eff} = L - \Delta L\) shrinks, and \(I_D \propto 1/L_{eff}\) grows. That is channel-length modulation (reader Sec. 8.5).

questions.prompt: A device has \(\lambda = 0.05\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\) and \(I_D \approx 200\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). Find \(r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)\) in kΩ.
questions.explanation: \(r_o = 1/(0.05\cdot200\ \mu\mathrm{A}) = 100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (reader Eq. 9.30). \(I_D\) here is the current without the \((1 + \lambda V_{DS})\) factor.
questions.figure_alt: NMOS output curves with channel-length modulation: after the knee at V_DS = V_ov each curve keeps rising slowly with V_DS instead of staying flat.

questions.prompt: Doubling the channel length (same \(W/L\) ratio, same current) does what to \(r_o\), roughly?
questions.explanation: The same \(\Delta L\) is a smaller fraction of a longer channel: \(\lambda \approx \Delta L/(L\,\Delta V)\). Long devices are used where high \(r_o\) is needed.

questions.prompt: A device draws \(100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) at \(V_{DS} = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\) in saturation, with \(\lambda = 0.1\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\). What is \(I_D\) (µA) at \(V_{DS} = 2\ \mathrm{V}\)?
questions.explanation: \(I_D \propto 1 + \lambda V_{DS}\): \(100\cdot1.2/1.05 \approx 114.3\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). Adding \(\Delta V/r_o\) with \(r_o\) computed from 100 µA gives about 115 µA, close but not exact.
questions.figure_alt: NMOS output curves with channel-length modulation: after the knee at V_DS = V_ov each curve keeps rising slowly with V_DS instead of staying flat.

questions.prompt: Measured in saturation: \(100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) at \(V_{DS} = 1\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(105\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) at \(2\ \mathrm{V}\). Extrapolating the line, at what negative \(V_{DS}\) does it reach zero? Give \(1/\lambda\) in V.
questions.explanation: Slope \(5\ \mu\mathrm{A/V}\); zero at \(1 - 100/5 = -19\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(1/\lambda = 19\ \mathrm{V}\) (\(\lambda \approx 0.053\)). Using the 2 V point's current alone (21 V) is off.
questions.figure_alt: Saturated NMOS current lines sloping upward (solid); their straight-line extensions (dashed) all meet the V_DS axis at -1/λ.

questions.prompt: Where do the extended saturated \(I_D\)-\(V_{DS}\) lines of one device meet?
options: At \(V_{DS} = -1/\lambda\) on the axis, whatever the gate voltage
questions.explanation: Each line is \(I_0(1 + \lambda V_{DS})\), zero at \(-1/\lambda\). It is the MOS counterpart of the BJT Early voltage.
questions.figure_alt: Saturated NMOS current lines sloping upward (solid); their straight-line extensions (dashed) all meet the V_DS axis at -1/λ.

questions.prompt: Find the intrinsic gain \(g_mr_o\) of a device at \(V_{ov} = 0.25\ \mathrm{V}\) with \(\lambda = 0.08\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\). (Use \(g_m = 2I_D/V_{ov}\) as a known prerequisite.)
questions.figure_alt: NMOS output curves with channel-length modulation: after the knee at V_DS = V_ov each curve keeps rising slowly with V_DS instead of staying flat.

questions.prompt: You double \(W\) (and the current) at fixed \(V_{ov}\) and \(L\). What happens to \(r_o\) and to \(g_mr_o\)?
questions.explanation: \(r_o \propto 1/I_D\) and \(g_m \propto I_D\) at fixed \(V_{ov}\), so their product depends only on \(\lambda\) and \(V_{ov}\).
questions.figure_alt: NMOS output curves with channel-length modulation: after the knee at V_DS = V_ov each curve keeps rising slowly with V_DS instead of staying flat.

questions.prompt: Preview of the small-signal model: where does \(r_o\) go in the MOSFET's linear model?
options: From drain to source, in parallel with the \(g_mv_{gs}\) source
questions.explanation: It models the slope \(\partial I_D/\partial V_{DS}\), a conductance between the same two terminals the current flows through.

questions.prompt: Preview of current mirrors: two identical devices with the same \(V_{GS}\) sit at \(V_{DS} = 0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(1.5\ \mathrm{V}\), \(\lambda = 0.1\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\). By what percent does the second current exceed the first?
questions.explanation: \(I_2/I_1 = (1 + 0.15)/(1 + 0.07) \approx 1.075\): about 7.5% more. Finite \(r_o\) is the main error source in simple mirrors.

questions.prompt: Preview of cascode sources: what is the standard way to get a current source with much more output resistance than one device's \(r_o\)?
options: Stack a second (common-gate) device on top, a cascode
questions.explanation: Parallel devices halve \(r_o\); shorter channels raise \(\lambda\). A cascode multiplies \(r_o\) by roughly \(g_mr_o\).
